chapters.title: Chapter 3: Energy, Commodities, and Global Chokepoints

lessons.title: Global Chokepoints: The Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, and the Cost of Disrupted Shipping

body.text: A handful of narrow waterways carry a hugely disproportionate share of the world's oil and trade. Threaten one of them, and the shock does not stay local, it reroutes ships, lifts freight rates, and moves crude prices within hours, well before any cargo actually stops moving.

children.text: A chokepoint, introduced back in Chapter 1, is a narrow, geographically fixed passage that a large share of global trade or energy must physically pass through. There is no alternate route that does not add enormous time and cost, which is exactly what makes these locations so valuable to control and so damaging to disrupt. This lesson covers the two chokepoints that matter most to an Indian investor: the Strait of Hormuz, and the Red Sea route through the Bab-el-Mandeb strait.
The World's Chokepoints at a Glance

cells: A large share of the world's seaborne crude oil and LNG exports out of the Gulf
A significant share of India's crude and LNG imports originate from Gulf producers and pass through this exact strait
A major share of Asia-bound oil and general trade, connecting the Indian Ocean to the South China Sea
Relevant to India's own trade with East and Southeast Asia, and a chokepoint China itself depends heavily on for energy imports
The route connecting the Suez Canal to the Indian Ocean, carrying a large share of Asia-Europe trade
A key route for Indian exports, especially textiles and manufactured goods, bound for European markets
Trade between the Atlantic and Pacific, especially for the Americas
Less directly relevant to India, but a reminder that chokepoint risk is not only geopolitical, a 2023-2024 drought forced the canal to restrict transits purely due to low water levels
Grain and energy exports out of the Black Sea, including from Russia and Ukraine
Connects back to the food-channel effects of the Russia-Ukraine war discussed in Chapter 1

children.text: Strait of Hormuz: The One That Would Matter Most to India

The Strait of Hormuz, between Iran and Oman, is arguably the single most important chokepoint for India specifically, given how much Gulf crude and LNG India sources and how directly it must pass through this narrow passage. Iran has periodically threatened to close or disrupt the strait during periods of heightened tension with the US and its allies, and while a full closure has never actually happened for a sustained period, even the credible threat of one is enough to spike crude prices, because oil markets price risk, not just realised disruption. An actual closure, even a brief one, would be one of the most severe supply shocks the global oil market could experience, given how few alternative routes exist for that much crude to reach the market.

body.text: This is the clearest example in this course of markets pricing a threat, not an event. Crude prices can jump meaningfully on a credible threat to close Hormuz, and give most of that gain back once tensions ease, even if the strait itself was never actually closed for a single day.

children.text: The Red Sea Crisis: A Live Case Study Since Late 2023

Since late 2023, Houthi forces in Yemen have repeatedly attacked commercial shipping in the Red Sea and the Bab-el-Mandeb strait, in the context of the broader Israel-Gaza conflict. In response, a large share of container shipping between Asia and Europe diverted away from the Suez Canal entirely, rerouting around the Cape of Good Hope at the southern tip of Africa instead. This single decision by shipping lines, not a physical blockage of the canal itself, shows how a threat to a chokepoint can shut down normal routing even without the chokepoint being literally closed.

stats.label: Extra transit time
stats.context: Additional sailing time for ships rerouting around the Cape of Good Hope instead of through the Suez Canal and Red Sea

stats.label: Freight rates
stats.context: Container freight rates on Asia-Europe routes increased substantially during the peak of the disruption, reported by multiple shipping trackers, though exact figures vary by route and have since moderated

stats.label: Most exposed Indian sectors
stats.context: Indian exporters shipping to Europe via this route faced both higher freight costs and longer, less predictable delivery times

body.text: This is a rare chokepoint disruption where India has not been purely a bystander. The Indian Navy has conducted anti-piracy and maritime security operations in the wider region during this period, reflecting how directly this chokepoint touches India's own trade and security interests, not just as a distant geopolitical headline.

body.title: Threat vs Actual Disruption
body.scenario: Tensions rise sharply near the Strait of Hormuz after a naval incident. No tankers have actually been blocked or attacked, but several shipping insurers announce they are reviewing coverage for vessels transiting the strait.
body.prompt: Based on this lesson, would you expect crude oil prices to react, even though no physical disruption has occurred yet? Why?
body.modelAnswer: Yes, very likely. Oil markets price risk and probability, not just realised events, as shown by how credible threats to Hormuz have historically moved crude prices even without an actual closure. Insurers reviewing coverage is itself a meaningful signal that professional risk assessors see elevated danger, which tends to accelerate the market's reaction rather than wait for an actual disruption to be confirmed.

body.title: What Actually Happened in the Red Sea
body.question: During the Red Sea shipping crisis from late 2023, what was the primary mechanism that disrupted trade?
options: The Suez Canal was physically blocked and closed to all traffic
Shipping lines voluntarily rerouted around the Cape of Good Hope in response to attack risk, adding significant time and cost
India imposed a trade embargo on Red Sea shipping routes
The Bab-el-Mandeb strait was drained due to a drought
body.explanation: The canal itself was not physically closed. Shipping lines made a commercial decision to avoid the attack risk in the Red Sea and Bab-el-Mandeb strait by rerouting around Africa, which alone was enough to raise costs and transit times significantly. The drought-related disruption described in this lesson refers to the separate Panama Canal, not the Red Sea.

cards.definition: The narrow waterway connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean, a critical link on the Asia-Europe shipping route via the Suez Canal.
Shipping lines choosing a longer, alternative path to avoid a risky or blocked chokepoint, trading higher cost and time for reduced risk.
The price charged to transport cargo by sea, which can spike sharply when chokepoint disruptions force rerouting or reduce available shipping capacity on a route.
Markets moving prices in response to the credible risk of a disruption, even before, or without, that disruption actually occurring.

points: A handful of narrow chokepoints, the Strait of Hormuz, the Strait of Malacca, and the Red Sea and Bab-el-Mandeb route, carry a hugely disproportionate share of global oil and trade, making them recurring flashpoints

The Strait of Hormuz matters most directly to India, given how much of its Gulf crude and LNG passes through it; even credible threats to close it have historically moved crude prices without an actual closure occurring

The Red Sea crisis since late 2023 shows how a threat alone, without a physical blockage, can redirect global shipping, adding roughly 10 to 14 days of transit time and raising freight rates sharply on affected routes
Indian exporters, particularly in textiles, apparel, and chemicals, have felt this directly through higher shipping costs and longer, less predictable delivery times to European markets
Chokepoint risk is not always geopolitical, the 2023-2024 Panama Canal disruption was driven by drought, a reminder that the same framework applies to non-political supply chain shocks too

body.text: Figures on chokepoint trade shares, freight rate increases, and transit time changes are approximate, based on widely reported estimates that vary by source and route, and can shift as conditions evolve. This lesson is educational and not investment, shipping, or logistics advice.
